summary.text: Choose the least time at which the Collatz orbit of a positive integer reaches 1; positivity and minimality imply that every earlier orbit value is greater than 1. Reading this finite orbit backward, recursively build an index—using one successor step at a nonbranching node and a parity bit at a branching node—so that the sequence decoder retraces the inverse Collatz edges from 1 to the original integer (with 1 itself represented by index 0).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C(x)=\begin{cases}
x/2,&x\equiv 0\pmod 2,\\
3x+1,&x\equiv 1\pmod 2
\end{cases}
\]
be the Collatz map on the nonnegative integers. We assume the Collatz conjecture in the form: for every positive integer \(m\), there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that \(C^k(m)=1\).

We first describe precisely the tree-evaluation function underlying the sequence. For nonnegative integers \(r,v\), let \(E(r,v)\) be defined recursively as follows. The value \(v\) is the current node and \(r\) is the remaining code.

* If \(r=0\), set \(E(r,v)=v\).
* If \(r>0\), put \(s=r-1\). Call \(v\) branching when
  \[
  v>4\qquad\text{and}\qquad v+2\equiv0\pmod 6.
  \]
  If \(v\) is branching, then
  \[
  E(r,v)=
  \begin{cases}
  E(s/2,2v),&s\text{ is even},\\
  E(s/2,(v-1)/3),&s\text{ is odd},
  \end{cases}
  \]
  where the divisions in the control parameter are integer divisions. If \(v\) is not branching, set
  \[
  E(r,v)=E(s,2v).
  \]

The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=E(n,1).
\]
The recursion terminates because when \(r>0\), its new control parameter is either \(r-1\) or \(\lfloor(r-1)/2\rfloor\), both strictly smaller than \(r\).

The main point is to show how to prepend one reverse Collatz step to any already encoded path.

For \(x,r\in\mathbb N\), put \(p=C(x)\), and define a new code \(I(x,r)\) by
\[
I(x,r)=
\begin{cases}
2r+1,&p\text{ is branching and }x\text{ is even},\\
2r+2,&p\text{ is branching and }x\text{ is odd},\\
r+1,&p\text{ is not branching}.
\end{cases}
\]
We claim that whenever \(x>1\),
\[
E(I(x,r),C(x))=E(r,x). \tag{1}
\]
Thus, starting at the parent \(C(x)\), the code \(I(x,r)\) first selects the child \(x\), after which it continues according to the old code \(r\).

We verify (1) by cases. First suppose that \(p=C(x)\) is branching.

If \(x\) is even, then \(I(x,r)=2r+1\). In evaluating \(E(2r+1,p)\), the code is first decremented to \(2r\). This is even, so at the branching node \(p\) the rule chooses the doubling child \(2p\), and the remaining code becomes
\[
(2r)/2=r.
\]
Since \(x\) is even,
\[
p=C(x)=x/2,
\]
and exact divisibility by \(2\) gives \(2p=x\). Consequently
\[
E(2r+1,p)=E(r,2p)=E(r,x).
\]

If \(x\) is odd, then \(I(x,r)=2r+2\). After the initial decrement, the code is \(2r+1\), which is odd. The branching rule therefore chooses the other child and leaves remaining code
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2r+1}{2}\right\rfloor=r.
\]
Here \(p=C(x)=3x+1\), so
\[
\frac{p-1}{3}=\frac{3x}{3}=x.
\]
It follows that
\[
E(2r+2,p)=E\left(r,\frac{p-1}{3}\right)=E(r,x).
\]

It remains to consider the case in which \(p=C(x)\) is not branching. We first show that in this case \(x\) must be even. Indeed, if \(x\) were odd, then because \(x>1\), we would have \(x\ge3\). Thus
\[
p=3x+1\ge10>4.
\]
Moreover, \(x+1\) is even, say \(x+1=2q\), and hence
\[
p+2=3x+3=3(x+1)=6q.
\]
Therefore \(p>4\) and \(p+2\) is divisible by \(6\), which says exactly that \(p\) is branching, a contradiction. Hence \(x\) is even.

Now \(I(x,r)=r+1\). Evaluating at the nonbranching node \(p\), the first action decrements the code to \(r\) and moves to the sole child \(2p\). Since \(x\) is even, \(p=C(x)=x/2\), and therefore \(2p=x\). Hence
\[
E(r+1,p)=E(r,2p)=E(r,x).
\]
This proves (1) in all cases.

We next use (1) repeatedly. We prove the following path-construction statement:

> If \(m,k\in\mathbb N\) and
> \[
> C^j(m)>1\quad\text{for every }j<k,
> \]
> then there exists a code \(n\) such that
> \[
> E(n,C^k(m))=m. \tag{2}
> \]

The proof is by induction on \(k\). If \(k=0\), take \(n=0\). Since \(C^0(m)=m\) and evaluation with zero code returns the current node,
\[
E(0,C^0(m))=E(0,m)=m.
\]

Now suppose the assertion is known for \(k\), and assume
\[
C^j(m)>1\qquad(j<k+1).
\]
In particular the same inequality holds for every \(j<k\), so by the induction hypothesis there is an \(r\) such that
\[
E(r,C^k(m))=m. \tag{3}
\]
Also, taking \(j=k\) in the assumption gives
\[
x:=C^k(m)>1.
\]
Apply the one-step identity (1) to this \(x\) and the code \(r\). Since
\[
C(x)=C(C^k(m))=C^{k+1}(m),
\]
we obtain
\[
E(I(x,r),C^{k+1}(m))
 =E(r,C^k(m))
 =m
\]
by (3). Thus \(n=I(C^k(m),r)\) proves (2) for \(k+1\), completing the induction.

We will also need the elementary fact that every iterate of a positive integer under \(C\) remains positive. For one step, if \(x>0\) is even, then in fact \(x\ge2\), so \(C(x)=x/2\ge1\). If \(x\) is odd, then \(C(x)=3x+1>0\). Induction on the number of iterations therefore gives
\[
m>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C^j(m)>0
\]
for every \(j\ge0\).

We can now prove the desired conditional surjectivity. Let \(m>0\). If \(m=1\), choose \(n=0\). Then
\[
a(0)=E(0,1)=1=m.
\]

Suppose instead that \(m\ne1\). By the assumed Collatz conjecture, there is some \(k\) for which \(C^k(m)=1\). Choose the least such \(k\). By minimality,
\[
C^j(m)\ne1\qquad\text{for every }j<k.
\]
Every such iterate is positive by the positivity result above. A positive integer unequal to \(1\) is greater than \(1\), so
\[
C^j(m)>1\qquad\text{for every }j<k.
\]
The path-construction statement (2) therefore supplies an integer \(n\) such that
\[
E(n,C^k(m))=m.
\]
But \(C^k(m)=1\), and hence
\[
a(n)=E(n,1)=E(n,C^k(m))=m.
\]

Thus, assuming the Collatz conjecture, every positive integer \(m\) occurs as a value of the sequence \(a(n)\).
